content.title: COOKING MISTAKES THAT QUIETLY DRAIN YOUR FOOD OF NUTRIENTS
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – This can leach over half its vitamin C into the water; steaming for 4-5 minutes keeps far more intact.
**Microwaving in plastic** – Heat can cause chemicals to migrate into your meal; switch to glass or ceramic containers before reheating.
**Draining and rinsing canned beans** – Skipping this step means you're eating extra sodium; a quick rinse cuts a large chunk of it away.
**Cooking tomatoes in a hurry** – A quick 2-3 minute simmer in olive oil actually boosts absorbable lycopene, so low heat for longer wins here.
**Using high heat for olive oil** – This breaks it down and creates compounds you don't want; save extra virgin olive oil for finishing, not frying.
**Soaking vegetables too long** – Letting cut produce sit in water pulls out water-soluble vitamins; prep and cook within 15-20 minutes instead.
**Tossing the cooking water** – Nutrients from steamed veggies end up in that liquid; save it for soups or sauces instead of pouring it down the drain.
**Overcooking eggs** – High heat for too long degrades some of the protein quality; a soft scramble or 7-minute boil preserves more.
**Skipping fat with salads** – Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K need oil to absorb; add 1 tbsp of olive oil or a few nuts to your greens.

content.caption:
Let's talk about broccoli, tomatoes, and olive oil, because these are the ones people get wrong most often. Broccoli loses a big chunk of its vitamin C the moment it hits boiling water, since that vitamin is water-soluble and literally dissolves out into the liquid around it. Tomatoes work the opposite way: lycopene is fat-soluble and bound tightly inside the cell walls, so a short simmer in oil actually breaks those walls down and makes more of it available to your body. And olive oil, once pushed past its smoke point, starts forming compounds linked to inflammation, which is why professional kitchens often reserve the good stuff for drizzling rather than frying.
